passage:
Subject: Thank you for Tuesday

Dear Pallavi,

Thank you for meeting me at the coffee counter. I came with three questions written on a card, and your answers were clear. First, skills: you said to get comfortable with spreadsheets and with writing short, clear updates. Second, entry paths: an internship in third year, or a junior analyst opening through campus placements. Third, daily work: mostly cleaning data in the mornings and meetings after lunch. I took notes on all of it, and next week I will compare them with what a second alumnus tells me. I have already signed up for a spreadsheet course. Thank you again for your time.

Best wishes,
Lokesh

qa.a: The three questions were about skills, entry paths and daily work.

qa.a: Lokesh probably felt keen but a little nervous, wanting to make good use of the time and get a clear picture for planning.

qa.q: What could Lokesh do with the notes next?
qa.a: Lokesh could compare them with the second alumnus's answers, see what matches, and choose a first step.

qa.q: How might Pallavi have felt on receiving a student with prepared questions?
qa.a: Pallavi may have felt pleased and respected, since the student took time to prepare.

passage: I'm Karthik, final year, and I want to tell you about the most useful coffee I ever had. I was stuck between physiotherapy and sports science, so I messaged an alumna, Vandana, who runs a clinic now. Before meeting her, I sat down and wrote exactly three questions. One: what skills matter most in her first two years? Two: which entry path would she pick today, the master's or a clinic job straight away? Three: what does a normal Tuesday look like for her? At the café I put my notebook on the table and wrote while she talked. She laughed and said most students just ask, "Is it a good career?" That evening I made two columns in my notebook and compared her answers with what my professor had told me.

qa.q: How many questions did Karthik write before the meeting?
How do you think Karthik felt going into the meeting?
qa.a: Karthik likely felt a little nervous but prepared and focused, since the questions were written and ready in the notebook.

qa.q: What else could Karthik do to get a fuller picture?
qa.a: Speak to one more person on the other path, sports science, with the same three questions, so the comparison is fair.

qa.q: How does Vandana see Karthik's approach?
qa.a: She seems amused and pleased; she laughs because most students only ask "Is it a good career?"

grounding: A student planning a career meets an alumna with three written questions and takes notes to compare later.

passage: My name's Jatin. I share a room with Aadhya at the hostel, and I watched how she got ready to meet the alumnus who works as an urban planner. The night before, she wasn't scrolling. She was writing on an index card, crossing out, rewriting. When I peeked, I saw three questions: skills to learn now, how people actually get their first job, and what a working day is like. In the morning she ironed a kurta, then read the card again on the bus. When she came back she had two pages of notes, underlined in two colours. She didn't say much about how it went. She just pinned the pages above her desk, next to her placement list, and started marking things off.

qa.q: Where did Aadhya write her questions?
qa.a: On an index card, the night before.

qa.q: What might Aadhya have been feeling, judging from the cues Jatin describes?
qa.a: She seemed serious and perhaps a bit nervous, rewriting her card and reading it again on the bus; she also seems determined afterwards.

qa.q: What could Aadhya try next time to get even more from such a meeting?
qa.a: She could send her three questions ahead, so the alumnus can think about them and give fuller answers.

qa.q: How might the alumnus see Aadhya's preparation?
qa.a: The alumnus would likely feel respected and find it easier to help, because her questions were clear and specific.

grounding: An observer describes a student preparing three questions for a professional and taking notes to compare later.
